translations.text: A homily for Holy Friday by our holy father John Chrysostom.
Our labor of fasting has now ended, and it has ended with the cross.
For where should the struggle for victory end, if not at the trophy of victory? For the cross is victorious.
It was planted once, but it continually drives away demons. For where are the pagan temples and the wasteful slaughter of animals?
Where are the pagan altars and the unholy fire? Everything was extinguished by one thing: the holy blood was shed.
And the cross stood firm: a mighty power, an invisible arrow, an immaterial medicine, a spring that relieves suffering, a glory subjected to scorn.
Even if I speak of other unheard-of things about Christ,
even if I astonish the listener by recounting unheard-of miracles,
I do not take as much pride in them as in the cross. For example, I might say this: Jesus came forth from a virgin.
It is a great miracle to bypass marriage and overturn nature. But if there had been no cross,
the first-created virgin would not have been saved by her deeds. But now, at the time of the cross, the first woman is saved,
healing the ancient evil through new gifts of grace. A dead man rose in Galilee, but he died again.
But I, having risen because of the cross, can no longer fall through death. Jesus, who is God, sailed the sea in a boat.
The wood gives help on that day, but I have received the wood as an everlasting good.
Taking it in place of a ship, I beat back the spiritual waves of the deceitful.
Five thousand were fed, though not by a single sign of the cross.
Where, then, are the leftovers of that food? How shall I, who was not there,
take the leftovers of those who were there? For twelve baskets of fragments remained.
For that gift of grace was limited in amount. Christ was crucified, and I am continually fed.
And though we are filled, we ask again; though we have received, we long for it, and our need grows greater. For grace suffers no depletion.
Let this day be praised, the parent of the world, because of which the other days were appointed for rejoicing. How?
Listen. Today Adam was created, on the sixth day. Today he bears the divine image.
Today a little creation was formed within creation. Today the human helmsman, the good oars of the inhabited world,
the living being who rules over all living beings. Today he received commandments, with freedom of choice.
Today he fell from [?]. Today he was admitted again. Oh, what a day of many forms!
O much-mourned and unmourned one! O you who brought sorrow in the morning but joy in the evening!
Indeed, you did not harm so much as heal. I confess to you that I was sorrowful as I recalled the sufferings of old,
hearing of Adam cast out of his Father's house—a man who was its citizen by birth, who lived without working the earth,
who was fed without rain, who needed no sweat or hoe or toil or running about to sustain his life,
who delighted in evergreen trees, passing from flower to flower, passing from fruit to fruit, with
what he needed following upon his thoughts, yet, because of the beauty of what he saw, unable [?] to decide where to stretch out his hands first.
I often shed tears when I saw him fallen away from such great blessings. For his suffering was shared,
and touched our whole race. But when I looked into the Gospel and came to this day—
for both that day and this were the sixth day—I cast my sorrow away and was changed, and my words are joyful.
And I say to myself and to you: pain and sorrow and sighing have fled away.
The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. For just as physicians' assistants
heal snakebites, taking healing herbs from them,
mixing them with the substances that caused the wounds and healing the injury, so the Savior also turned every evil cause to good,
making human bitterness sweet, turning it into healing, and turning the sting of death back upon death itself,
turning the injury caused by the tree into salvation. He took the day that had saddened the world,
and gave back a day that gladdened the world. Do not believe me, but your own eyes.
Look at this gathering, and stop [?] us with the day of the cross.
And we all rejoice, and we fast from evil, and we cleanse everything inward and outward.
Such is the meaning of the feast; such is the form of its joy. I will recount a few wonders of the cross's power. Look around the inhabited world:
how many villages and how many cities, how many places, how many nations, how many islands, how many rivers, how many coasts,
how many peoples and lands and foreigners! All these fast for the sake of the cross, having crucified their enemies by its power.
For many, the night comes to an end, but the toil of fasting does not end.
And now, why have we all gathered to hear something about the cross, and why do we fill the churches,
pushing one another, sweating and laboring? Often, before judges,
we are granted an audience, yet before Jesus we stand gladly.
Because Jesus stood for our sake, to halt the course of evil. What, then, happened today?
For we must not let the wonders of this day simply pass us by. There was moonlight, and it was just before dawn.
And he was led with his hands bound into Pilate's praetorium—hands that healed the blind,
and cured the lame. And his fingers were fastened with bonds,
the fingers that fashioned eyelids. And the healer of nature was held back
from completing his skillful work. Is this what you give the Lord in return? He was bound,
he who binds the waters in the clouds and releases those in fetters by his power.
He who grants release to captives was bound, he who freed Lazarus
from the bonds of death. He was led into prison,
he who is attended by angels beyond our knowledge, he whose throne is heaven.
And he endured being dragged along: the Creator by his creation, the Maker by what he had made,
the Creator by what he had created. What, then, came of this? What happened? “And they,” it says, “did not enter the prison,
so that they would not defile themselves, but might eat the Passover.” Oh, what great lawlessness!
They commit unjust murders, yet refuse to enter the prison, taking care not to defile themselves,
though they are already defiled, destroying one sheep with another.
So the Judge of the whole world awaited judgment. He awaited witnesses,
he who created the souls of the witnesses [?], and he was being judged. And human beings sat in judgment,
but God stood, and as he stood he remained silent, standing before human doors,
the Lord of heaven's doors. Pilate questioned them, more humane than the Jews in their malice. What shall I say?
Their malice will reveal the truth of what was done [?]. “What accusation do you bring against this man?
Who holds God guilty?” I am compelled to speak Pilate's words,
for Jesus is silent—not because the Word lacks words, but lest by answering he undo the crown of the cross.
Did he desire possessions, he who disregarded possessions? Or other people's houses, he who had nowhere to lay his head?
Or riches, he who stripped even his own disciples down to their belts, who had no donkey and took another person's donkey
so that he might bless your children? State the charge. Establish whether you were right to put him to death. The Jews answered him.
“If he were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you.” What great proof of his deeds! What a lawless answer!
State his wrongdoing, and do not [?] your hearers. Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.”
The wise judge shifted the burden onto the heads of the Jews: “You wicked men, take your accomplice.”
The Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.” How, then, did you kill Isaiah?
How did you kill Zechariah? How did you kill each of the prophets? But “We cannot put anyone to death” means not that they were unwilling,
but that they were unable. For the Romans had already deprived them of such authority. Thus it is being abolished,
the law, now existing only in ink but inactive in practice. Jesus abolished it even while bound.
But Pilate said, “I find no fault in him.” Not you alone, Pilate,
but neither do the Jews, nor the blind, nor the dead, nor the sun, nor the moon, nor creation,
nor all the righteous, the prophets and martyrs. The prophet says, “He committed no sin,
nor was deceit found in his mouth.” All speak with Pilate, giving him the title “Righteous.”
Only the Jews oppose him, arguing with shouts and seeking to obscure the truth with their uproar,
and confirming Isaiah’s words: “I expected it to produce grapes,
but it produced thorns; and not righteousness, but a cry of desolation.” The vineyard of the Jews,
bearing shouting as its fruit! While this was happening, Pilate could neither speak nor hear
because of the uproar of the assembled crowd, and he thought there would be a riot.
For his wife, a good helper, sent word to him, restraining her husband as he was being urged on,
saying, “Have nothing to do with that righteous man. If you can, release him; but if you cannot, save yourself.”
She was all but saying David’s words: “Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly,
or my life with bloodthirsty men.” “Have nothing to do with that righteous man,
for I have suffered much in a dream because of him.” Another Joseph, seeing the truth in dreams,
testifying against the shouting of the Jews! For it was fitting that they should be defeated by a woman.
Rahab the prostitute defeated them. The woman with the flow of blood defeated them. The Canaanite woman defeated them.
And now once again a woman stands firm against them. The Jews answered him, “We have a law,
and according to our law he must die.” What law? By what words is it confirmed?
[?] with those honored today. He was led like a sheep to slaughter.
And like an innocent lamb, he was silent before the one shearing him.
He does not open his mouth. Because of the lawlessness of my people, he was led to death.
I find these words applicable here, and nowhere else: Jesus,
truly being put to death. Pilate entered the praetorium, yielding to the fury of the Jews.
Trying to extinguish the unquenchable flame, he went in and came out. He kindled the fire still more.
For he came out bringing Jesus, crowned and clothed in purple, already victorious,
already clothed in royal guise. What was being done was intended as mockery,
but the image accorded with the true nature of his kingship. And so, when they saw him whom they had often seen,
whom they had never seen, whom they continually see and become inflamed, burning with their own fire—
for it would have been better if they had burned in the fire—they raised their Sodom-like cry.
They rose up in a frenzy: “Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!” “Do you want me to crucify your king?”
“We have no king but Caesar,” they said. Renunciation without persecution! Godlessness joined with the evil of Egypt!
“Are these your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt?” Do you have no king but Caesar?
Who, then, led you through the wilderness? Who fed you? Whom does Moses invoke when he says,
“The Lord reigns forever and ever, and beyond”? Since, then, you have rejected your own king,
remain without a king, dragging the eternal yoke of slavery.
This took place until the sixth hour. Let us also look at the remaining part of the day.
For the whole day is holy. They took him, crowned. With what thorns? With the Jews’
rewards. “I expected it to produce wine for me, but it produced thorns.” He was struck in the face. He received wounds, but he was put to shame by nothing.
Stand with Jesus and see God through his eyes. For what did he say? “Lord, who has believed our report?”
“We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty, but his appearance was dishonored,
wasting away more than the sons of men.” Did he not possess every kind of beauty, the maker of beauty?
For he wept over the evils of the Jews, being a man under affliction and knowing how to endure pain—a man, not God.
For it was a man, not God, who was being wounded. Who, then, is this man of many sorrows and many hardships?
and cast out by everyone. Is what he suffers perhaps just? He bears our sins.
And he accepts suffering for us. I find no fault in this man.
But do not be ashamed of the humiliating [?]. Though he suffered so much, he remained free from suffering. He was wounded.
He was spat upon. He suffered dishonor, yet he himself remains honored and glorious. Of those who sin,
as someone, Isaiah, said to them: “And we thought him to be in pain and wounded
and afflicted. But he was wounded because of our sins, and he suffered because of our lawless deeds.
Is it he, then, [?] and we are wounded by him? By his wound we were healed.
A dead man, a physician to the dead; a wounded man, a physician to people suffering many pains.
An herb to counter the wound. But how long will you flatter our indifference, O man?
Say plainly what is being sought. Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb.
A good sheep, handed over to wicked cooks, is slaughtered. O Jews, do not shear the sheep.
But if you do shear it, spare the sheep that bears good fruit. And others were also being led with him,
two evildoers. For our discourse comes to the tenth hour of the day. Let no one condemn his own life.
I did indeed intend to pass over the story, since I have told it to you many times. But I see the robber continually compelling me.
And no wonder. For he also forced open the gates of [?], cleverly turning the Savior away from us.
The Lamb and two wolves stood on the cross. But one remained earthly in his disposition,
while the other was already being transformed, saying, “Remember me when you come in your kingdom.”
O the power of Jesus! A robber is already a prophet, preaching from the cross:
“Remember me, Lord, when you come in your kingdom.” For what do you see that is royal, O robber?
The blows, or the spitting? The nails, or the wood?
And the taunts of the Jews, and the spear already being drawn by a soldier?
“But I see,” he said, “his angels standing around him. I see the sun fleeing,
the curtain being torn, the earth trembling,
the dead already preparing to flee.” Jesus, who accepts everyone, who also to those who came at the eleventh
hour gave the same denarius: “Truly, truly, I say to you.” You too, O robber, receive this “truly.”
He who today is a robber is today a son. Today you will be with me in paradise.
I, who drove you out, will bring you in—I who shut the gates of paradise,
who fenced it off with a flaming spear. For unless I bring you in, the gates will remain shut.
Come, O robber, having plundered the devil and been crowned over him, having seen a man and bowed down to God,
having cast away your former weapon and taken up the weapon of faith. With these things being so,
and everything illuminated: from the air, the sun; from the gardens, the tree;
from the Jews, gall; from woven fabrics, the seamless robe; from the sea, the purple garment;
from the mines, iron—the spear and the nails. And with the twin streams
of blood and water poured out, the Savior was doing his work: “Father, forgive them their sin.”
Whom did he forgive? The Greeks or the Jews? Strangers or foreigners? Everyone, without distinction.
For he spoke once, and the deed is continually accomplished. Did he say “Forgive” about the soldiers alone?
He speaks throughout all ages, and he speaks continually, and whoever wishes receives.
They all assembled in Pilate’s praetorium, saying what?
“We know that that deceiver said while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise.’” Do you know this so well?
Do you remember so well that he will rise? He secures the tomb. For you are securing it for me. Guard
the dead man so that he does not escape. “You have a guard,” he said. “Go and secure it as you know how.”
You killed him as you knew how; arrange things as you know how. Keep watch. For if you had not guarded him,
you would have left me grounds for an argument. But now I hand him over to you yourselves.
When he was alive, he was held by you; but when he was killed, he was hidden from all of you.
Let us therefore remain watchful, not sleeping, so that we may see the deep sleep of the Jews
and celebrate with the heavenly hosts in Christ Jesus our Lord,
to whom belong glory and dominion, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
